title: The Normal Distribution
intro: The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the shape of sums of many small independent effects. Every normal is a shifted, stretched copy of one standard normal, so one table, or one function, covers them all.

blocks.caption: The N(μ, σ²) density: mean μ, variance σ².

blocks.text: The standard normal $Z\sim N(0, 1)$ has density $\varphi(z) = e^{-z^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ and CDF $\Phi(z)$, which has no closed form. Any $X\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is $\mu + \sigma Z$, so $P(X\le x) = \Phi((x - \mu)/\sigma)$: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation, look up $\Phi$. That subtraction and division, standardisation, is the most-used calculation in statistics.

items: About 68.3% of the probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean, 95.4% within two and 99.7% within three.
The two-sided 95% point is $1.96\sigma$; the one-sided 95% point is $1.645\sigma$.

Tails fall off faster than exponentially: $P(Z > t)\approx\varphi(t)/t$ for large $t$. Six-sigma events have probability about $10^{-9}$, which is why heavy-tailed data (finance, networks) badly embarrass normal models.

The central limit theorem: standardised sums of many independent variables with finite variance are approximately normal, whatever they are individually (The Central Limit Theorem (#/probability/limit-theorems/central-limit-theorem)).

Closure: linear combinations of independent (indeed of jointly) normal variables are normal, so normal models stay normal under linear operations (The Multivariate Normal (#/probability/multivariate/multivariate-normal)).

Maximum entropy: among all distributions with a given mean and variance, the normal has the largest entropy (Entropy and Information (#/probability/toolkit/entropy)). It assumes the least beyond those two numbers.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    print(f"P(|Z| < {k}) = {stats.norm.cdf(k) - stats.norm.cdf(-k):.4f}")
print(f"z for a 95% two-sided interval: {stats.norm.ppf(0.975):.4f}")
# Standardising: heights ~ N(170, 8^2). P(H > 185)?
mu, sd = 170, 8
print(f"P(H > 185) = P(Z > {(185 - mu) / sd:.3f}) = {1 - stats.norm.cdf((185 - mu) / sd):.4f}")
# Sums of independent normals are normal; a linear combination keeps normality
rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
a, b = rng.normal(1, 2, 10 ** 6), rng.normal(-3, 1, 10 ** 6)
c = 2 * a - b
print(f"2A - B: mean {c.mean():.3f} (5), variance {c.var():.3f} (4*4 + 1 = 17), excess kurtosis {stats.kurtosis(c):+.3f}")
# The normal tail is light: P(Z > t) compared with the bound phi(t)/t
for t in (2, 4, 6):
    print(f"P(Z > {t}) = {stats.norm.sf(t):.3e},  phi(t)/t = {stats.norm.pdf(t) / t:.3e}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: $P(\vert Z\vert < 1, 2, 3) = 0.6827, 0.9545, 0.9973$, and the 97.5% point is 1.9600. With heights $N(170, 8^2)$, $P(H > 185) = P(Z > 1.875) = 0.0304$. The combination $2A - B$ of independent normals has mean 5.00, variance 17.01 and excess kurtosis 0.001 (normal). The tail ratio $\varphi(t)/t$ overestimates $P(Z > t)$ by 19% at $t = 2$, 6% at 4 and 3% at 6.

blocks.title: Exam scores
blocks.text: IQ scores are modelled as $N(100, 15^2)$. What fraction exceed 130? What score is the 90th percentile?

blocks.title: Which is larger
blocks.text: $X\sim N(2, 9)$ and $Y\sim N(1, 16)$ are independent. Find $P(X > Y)$.

blocks.title: The normalising constant
solution: Square it and write the product as a double integral: $I^2 = \iint e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}\,dx\,dy$.
